<pre-registration>
    <metadata>
        <title>Error Distribution Parameters in Visual Working Memory as Predictors of Visuospatial Cognitive Performance</title>
        <description>An experimental study examining whether individual differences in visual working memory error distributions, characterized by concentration parameters from von Mises circular statistical models, predict mental rotation performance and visual imagery vividness. Participants complete orientation recall tasks, mental rotation tests, and imagery questionnaires to test whether distributional precision parameters capture meaningful cognitive differences beyond simple accuracy measures.</description>
        <contributors>Research team to be specified</contributors>

        <license type="select_one">
            CC-By Attribution 4.0 International
        </license>

        <subject>Cognitive Psychology, Experimental Psychology, Individual Differences, Spatial Cognition, Working Memory, Circular Statistics, Psychometrics</subject>
        <tags>visual working memory, mental rotation, circular statistics, individual differences, spatial cognition, error distributions, precision parameters, von Mises distribution, visuospatial abilities</tags>
    </metadata>

    <study_information>
        <hypotheses>H1: Individual differences in visual working memory precision, operationalized as concentration parameters (κ) from von Mises distributions fitted to orientation recall errors, will positively predict mental rotation accuracy (Directional hypothesis: higher κ values predict higher MRT accuracy). This hypothesis is grounded in theories suggesting that spatial working memory precision reflects domain-general mechanisms for maintaining and manipulating spatial representations that are critical for mental rotation transformations.

H2: VWM concentration parameters will more strongly predict mental rotation performance at larger rotation angles (100° and 150°) compared to smaller angles (0° and 50°), evidenced by significant κ × rotation angle interactions (Directional hypothesis: stronger κ-performance relationships at larger rotations). This is theoretically justified by the incremental rotation hypothesis, which suggests that larger rotations require more precise maintenance of intermediate spatial states during transformation.

H3: VWM concentration parameters will positively correlate with VVIQ2 total imagery vividness scores (Directional hypothesis: higher κ values predict higher VVIQ2 scores). This hypothesis assumes that both VWM precision and imagery vividness reflect shared mechanisms for maintaining detailed spatial representations, though this connection requires empirical validation given potential differences between objective precision and subjective vividness ratings.

H4: These κ-performance relationships will persist after controlling for general cognitive factors including processing speed (response time variability) and task engagement (focus loss metrics), but NOT after controlling for mean VWM accuracy due to mathematical dependencies (Directional hypothesis: κ maintains predictive power beyond speed and engagement factors but not beyond accuracy).</hypotheses>
    </study_information>

    <design_plan>
        <study_type type="select_one">
            Experiment
        </study_type>

        <blinding type="select_multiple">
            - Personnel who analyze the data collected from the study are not aware of the treatment applied to any given group.
        </blinding>
        
        <additional_blinding>No additional blinding beyond data analysis blinding</additional_blinding>
        <study_design>Mixed experimental design with within-subjects factors for both VWM and mental rotation tasks. VWM task uses a 2×2 factorial design (set size: 2 vs 4 items × delay: 1000ms vs 4000ms) across 120 trials plus 6 attention checks. Mental rotation task uses a within-subjects design with rotation angle (0°, 50°, 100°, 150°) and reflection state (same vs different) across 96 trials plus 6 attention checks (12 shapes × 4 angles × 2 reflection states). Task order is counterbalanced between participants (VWM first vs MRT first) via random assignment. VVIQ2 questionnaire follows cognitive tasks. The design is nested with trials within conditions within participants.</study_design>
        <randomization>Simple randomization will assign participants to one of two task order conditions (VWM-first or MRT-first) using JavaScript code 'if (Math.random() < 0.5)...' implemented in the Pavlovia platform. Within each task, trial presentation order will be fully randomized for each participant using the platform's built-in randomization functions.</randomization>
    </design_plan>

    <sampling_plan>
        <existing_data type="select_one">
            Registration prior to creation of data
        </existing_data>
        
        <data_collection_procedures>Participants will be recruited via Prolific with inclusion criteria: adults aged 18-35, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, no hearing deficits, using laptop or desktop computer. Prolific's pre-screening filters will enforce these criteria. Payment will be pro-rated at £9/hour for estimated 40-minute session duration. The experiment will be implemented on Pavlovia.org with minimum browser dimension requirements (768×768 pixels) enforced before participation begins. Upon completion of cognitive tasks, participants will be redirected to VVIQ2 questionnaire on SurveyMonkey. Data logging will capture all trial-level variables, practice attempts, and engagement metadata including aggregate focus loss instances and duration during instructions and trials.</data_collection_procedures>
        <sample_size>Target sample size is 713 participants</sample_size>
        <sample_size_rationale>Power analysis using the pwr package in R targeted detection of small-to-medium effect size (f² = 0.02) with 80% power at α = 0.05 for mixed-effects models. Initial calculated sample size was 549 participants. Final sample size of 713 includes 30% inflation to account for anticipated attrition and exclusions in online testing environment. Given the extensive exclusion criteria (VWM practice accuracy, attention checks, MRT practice accuracy, timeout rates, focus loss thresholds), actual data loss may exceed 30%, potentially requiring additional recruitment.</sample_size_rationale>
        <stopping_rule>Data collection will continue until 713 participants complete the full experimental protocol or until recruitment budget is exhausted, whichever occurs first. If analyzable sample falls below 549 participants due to exclusions, additional recruitment will be conducted.</stopping_rule>
    </sampling_plan>

    <variables>
        <manipulated_variables>VWM task: Set size (2 vs 4 items) and delay duration (1000ms vs 4000ms) manipulated factorially within-subjects across 120 base trials. Mental rotation task: Rotation angle (0°, 50°, 100°, 150°) and reflection state (same vs different orientation) manipulated within-subjects across 96 base trials (12 unique shapes × 4 angles × 2 reflection states). Task order (VWM first vs MRT first) manipulated between-subjects via random assignment.</manipulated_variables>
        <measured_variables>VWM precision parameters: Concentration parameter (κ) and bias parameter (μ) from von Mises distributions fitted to orientation recall errors using maximum likelihood estimation after mixture modeling to separate memory-based from guess responses. Mental rotation performance: Trial-level accuracy (correct/incorrect binary responses) and reaction times (milliseconds from stimulus onset to keypress) on correct trials only. VVIQ2 scores: Total score (sum of 32 items rated 1-5, range 32-160) and eight subscale scores (sum of 4 items each, range 4-20) corresponding to different imagery scenarios. Engagement metrics: Total instances and duration of focus loss during instruction screens and during task trials (4 aggregate values), task timeout rates, attention check accuracy. Response time variability: Coefficient of variation for reaction times calculated separately for each task on correct trials only.</measured_variables>
        <indices>VWM precision index: Concentration parameter (κ) from von Mises distribution fitted to orientation recall errors after applying two-component mixture model (von Mises + uniform) to identify and exclude guess responses, then refitting von Mises using maximum likelihood estimation on non-guess trials only. VVIQ2 total index: Sum of all 32 questionnaire items (range 32-160). VVIQ2 subscale indices: Eight separate sums of 4 items each corresponding to familiar person, sunrise, shop front, countryside scene, driving scenario, beach scene, railway station, and garden scene (range 4-20 per subscale). Response time variability index: Coefficient of variation (standard deviation/mean) calculated separately for VWM and MRT tasks using correct trials only.</indices>
    </variables>

    <analysis_plan>
        <statistical_models>Primary analyses will use generalized linear mixed-effects models to test VWM precision (κ) as predictor of mental rotation performance. Model 1: Logistic mixed-effects model predicting trial-level MRT accuracy with fixed effects for κ (z-scored), rotation angle (0°, 50°, 100°, 150° as ordered factor), and their interaction, plus random intercepts and random slopes for rotation angle by participant to account for individual differences in rotation difficulty effects. Model 2: Linear mixed-effects model predicting log-transformed RT on correct MRT trials with identical fixed and random effects structure. Control analyses will include RT variability and focus loss metrics as covariates but will NOT include mean VWM accuracy due to mathematical dependencies with κ. Secondary analysis will use multiple regression predicting VVIQ2 total score from κ with RT variability and focus loss metrics as covariates. Exploratory analyses will examine κ relationships with individual VVIQ2 subscales and test alternative circular distributions (wrapped normal, wrapped Cauchy) using AIC/BIC model comparison at the group level.</statistical_models>
        <transformations>Orientation recall errors will be converted to circular coordinates (radians) before von Mises fitting. Reaction times will be log-transformed to address positive skew. κ parameters and control variables will be z-scored for inclusion in mixed-effects models. Rotation angle will be coded as ordered factor (0°, 50°, 100°, 150°) to test linear trends in interaction effects.</transformations>
        <inference_criteria>Two-tailed tests with α = 0.05 for all analyses. False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction using Benjamini-Hochberg procedure will be applied separately to: (1) fixed effects in mixed-effects models, (2) VVIQ2 subscale analyses. Effect sizes will include marginal and conditional R² for mixed-effects models, standardized beta coefficients for regressions, and 95% confidence intervals for all key estimates. For logistic models, odds ratios will be reported with confidence intervals.</inference_criteria>
        <data_exclusion>Participant exclusions: Overall task timeout rate >20% in either task, total focus loss instances >10 across all trials (fixed threshold), failure to meet VWM practice accuracy criterion (average absolute error ≥30°), VWM attention check accuracy <80% (errors >45° on Set Size 1 trials), MRT practice accuracy <66% (8/12 correct), or MRT accuracy on 0° rotation trials <70%. Trial-level exclusions: Reaction times <500ms or >7000ms for MRT (revised thresholds appropriate for spatial transformation task), reaction times <200ms or >7000ms for VWM, and timeout trials. Outliers meeting statistical criteria (>3.29 SD from mean) will be removed entirely, not winsorized.</data_exclusion>
        <missing_data>VVIQ2 participants with >10% missing items or invariant response patterns (identical ratings across all 32 items) will be excluded. No imputation planned as all cognitive task measures are required fields in the online platform.</missing_data>
        <exploratory_analysis>We will explore whether mixture modeling parameters (guess rate) independently predict performance measures beyond κ parameters. Additional analyses may examine task order effects and their interactions with precision-performance relationships, test split-half reliability of κ parameters across trial subsets, and assess whether browser technical factors (frame rate) moderate key relationships. Sensitivity analyses will test robustness across different exclusion criteria and parameter estimation methods.</exploratory_analysis>
    </analysis_plan>

    <other>This research bridges cognitive psychology, psychometrics, and computational modeling by connecting behavioral error distributions to individual differences in spatial abilities. The circular statistical framework draws from directional statistics while mixed-effects modeling incorporates advances from computational cognitive science. Critical limitations include the correlational design preventing causal inferences about cognitive mechanisms, potential mathematical dependencies between κ and accuracy measures, and reliance on behavioral data without direct neural measurement. Findings could inform educational psychology regarding spatial ability assessment and contribute to computational models of visual working memory, though claims about underlying cognitive architecture must be interpreted cautiously given these methodological constraints.</other>
</pre-registration>
